question: Compare the effectiveness of voucher systems and tax incentives in reducing undeclared domestic work across EU Member States, highlighting differences in coverage and equity impacts.
reference: Voucher systems are generally more effective in reducing undeclared domestic work across EU Member States, as they simplify formal employment and make it more affordable, leading to a noticeable decline in informal work. They are broader in coverage and tend to be fairer, though they still face challenges in reaching low-income families. In contrast, tax incentives primarily benefit wealthier households and have a limited impact on reducing undeclared work, with a core criticism being their regressive effect on employing households. Both systems have limitations, but voucher systems are more effective in promoting formal employment and equity.

Voucher systems show mixed but sometimes substantial effects, while the evidence on tax incentives is also uneven. In the synthesis report, experts describe voucher impacts as generally low in Austria, Belgium and Greece: Austria’s vouchers were scarcely used, and the Belgian study estimated that less than 10% of voucher-paid domestic work had previously been undeclared. Sweden’s RUT vouchers were associated with low undeclared-work levels, but the relationship was not substantiated (page 286: “the impact of the use of vouchers on undeclared work is generally quite low”; page 287: “this relationship remains to be substantiated”). Other evidence gives stronger results for specific schemes: Belgium’s service vouchers were reported to have halved undeclared work in covered activities, and France’s CESU system was associated with a fall in informal employment from about 50% in 1996 to 20% in 2015 (pages 188 and 187).

Tax incentives also vary in effectiveness. The synthesis report says they had little effect in Germany, whereas Spain saw an increase in declared domestic workers after their introduction in 2011, although that increase later plateaued (page 287: “in Germany the ESPAN experts explain that tax incentives have had little effect”; “an increase in the number of declared domestic workers”).

Coverage differs by design. Vouchers can provide a traceable payment and declaration route, and some schemes directly target domestic or care services; Belgium’s scheme, for example, covered around 150,000 workers by 2014 and served approximately one million users. Tax incentives reduce the cost of declared employment, sometimes alongside vouchers, but their generosity differs across countries: Portugal’s deduction was 5%, while most Member States using such incentives applied 20% (pages 188 and 285).

The clearest equity concern in the cited evidence is with tax relief: in Germany, benefits depend on taxable household income, so households with little or no income tax benefit less or not at all; in Sweden, the highest-income decile received 40% of the total tax deduction (page 287: “the wealthier the household, the greater the relief”; “the highest income decile group benefited from 40%”). Voucher systems are not automatically equitable either: the France discussion says tax advantages primarily benefited higher-income households, particularly the top 10% (page 187). Overall, the pages suggest that effectiveness and equity depend on scheme design and country context; they do not establish that one instrument is consistently superior across EU Member States.
